Inner City Hope

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In the shadow of Johannesburg’s decaying Ellis Park precinct, one man’s love for tennis is reviving forgotten courts and giving new life to a fading sport.

Unique Selling Point:
At the crumbling tennis courts near Ellis Park, Johannesburg, one man is fighting a lonely but determined battle to save a sport he loves. Alec Galanakis — a passionate tennis historian, teacher, and lifelong player — has devoted his life to reviving tennis in the inner city and protecting courts that once stood as proud monuments of South Africa’s sporting culture.

In a landscape marked by decay and neglect, Alec’s mission is twofold: to keep the heritage of Johannesburg’s iconic courts alive and to pass the beauty and discipline of tennis on to a new generation. His initiative has transformed forgotten spaces into sanctuaries where children discover not only a sport, but dignity, purpose, and hope.

Further information:
Why This Story Matters

Cultural Heritage: The Ellis Park precinct is synonymous with South Africa’s rich sporting history. Allowing these courts to decay means erasing a piece of Johannesburg’s identity.

Human Spirit: Alec’s sacrifice — leaving his teaching career to dedicate himself full-time to this mission — shows the power of one person’s passion to revive a forgotten dream.

Social Relevance: In a city battling urban decline, crime, and hopelessness, Alec’s tennis initiative offers children a safe space and an alternative path.

Visual Impact: The contrast between the decaying courts and the vibrant energy of children playing on them creates striking imagery — a metaphor for resilience and rebirth.

Extra Budget Items:
Security for shooting downtown Johannesburg.

Script:


(Commentator) Welcome to the South African Open in this prestigious venue, Johannesburg, Ellis Park. Quiet please.



(Alec) You can almost still hear it…This place, it’s seen it all. History was made on this court. But even in its silence, there’s still something here.



(Claire) They call her The Old Lady of Tennis – Ellis Park. For more than a century, these courts rang with serves from legends like Billie Jean King and Arthur Ashe. Today, the courts are worn, the stands are empty and her future uncertain.



(Claire) She’s easy to miss, tucked beside the imposing rugby stadium next door. Built in 1923, Ellis Park was once the heartbeat of South African tennis – home to national championships, host to international stars, and even considered the world’s fifth Grand Slam venue.



(Claire) But like the suburbs around her – once vibrant, now scarred by crime, decay and neglect – she too has been forgotten.



(Claire) Hello.



(Claire) But one man’s obsession may be the key to her survival.



(Claire) So, yeah. That’s my cool tennis story.



(Claire) A former teacher and tennis coach, Alec Galanakis has always carried Ellis Park close to his heart.



(Claire) At what point did even, for you personally, Ellis Park come on your radar?



(Alec) Ellis Park was always this thing far away. I mean, I was lucky enough to go and watch a few matches there at the SA Open. It was absolutely massive. One year, it was the second-largest tournament in the world after Wimbledon. 



(Alec) We won the Federation Cup of the year, so that’s like the world cup of tennis for the women. And there was chaos, it was chock-a-block; 126 000 people coming to watch the top players in the world.



(Alec) So, the late 70s and the 80s were when tennis was booming in South Africa.



(Claire) But over the years, it slipped into decline.



(Alec) People didn't want to go there to play tennis because they felt it was dangerous, and the suburbs was falling apart.



(Claire) When the city threatened to demolish it to build housing, Alec was determined to fight back. He became an amateur historian, piecing together Ellis Park’s forgotten story.



(Alec) Ten years ago, I started thinking, “Well, the history behind it is unbelievable. How can I save this place?” But by learning the history of it and doing the research… And I would go to William Cullen Library at Wits there, in the archives, go and do that and get those old Rand Daily Mails out and those beautiful old things.



(Claire) He hoped that, by proving its historic significance, Ellis Park would be declared a heritage site.



(Claire) Life downtown is tough, marked by unemployment, poverty and crime. Last year, Alec left his teaching job to launch the Joburg Tennis Rejuvenation Programme, bringing coaching and hope to inner-city youth and giving the courts a new purpose. He coaches four days a week and, thanks to donations, provides the children with rackets and shoes.



(Claire) This is the place where the children come from, right?



(Alec) Absolutely.



(Claire) This is their reality. And it does feel a world away from a tennis court.



(Alec) Yeah, it's miles. I mean, you've got two streets and then you've got this beautiful stadium over there. They are miles apart. All of these kids have never seen those courts before since this, year. And none of them have ever had the opportunity to go down and play on those courts. They have absolutely nothing. They come and play in their school shoes, and sometimes they take the shoes off and run through their socks.



(Claire) The programme is already changing lives; 20-year-old Moses Nkabinde is one of its first success stories.



(Claire) Hello, hello.



(Moses) How are you, ma’am?



(Claire) Very well thanks, Moses. Good to meet you.



(Moses) Are you ready for tennis today?



(Claire) I’m ready to watch you play tennis.



(Moses) Okay. That’s okay.



(Claire) Do people that see you walking around get the fact that you're playing tennis, you’re carrying rackets?



(Moses) People used to say, “Oh, you’re Djokovic. Oh, you’re Federer. Oh, you’re Alcaraz,” when they were watching the Grand Slam. So, it was actually nice.



(Claire) With poverty and hardship at home, tennis became an escape for Moses.



(Claire) So, how did you get introduced to tennis and how did you start loving it?



(Moses) I was just running away from the situation at home – just wanted to forget about it. Because I was young, I was like 16, 15. Honestly, me and my brother were in a tight spot at that time. My mom told us to go sell some clothes in Hillbrow and I didn’t like it at all. And I said, “You know what? Let’s go find something to do.” I just said, “Okay, why not have fun here on the court and just forget about what’s happening at home?” So, yeah… That’s why I mainly started tennis.



(Claire) Sadly, his ultimate ambition was unfulfilled.



(Moses) The goal was to play college tennis before. But then, because I never finished school and all of that, the opportunity was never there. I wanted to be one of the known coaches in the world actually.



(Claire) Recognising his talent, Alec took Moses under his wing.



(Claire) Through the programme, Moses earned his coaching certificate, trained formally and now coaches at a top tennis club in Sandton.



(Claire) Let me stand by the net.



(Claire) But he hasn't forgotten what made that all possible.



(Claire) It’s 2 PM. School’s out and, for Alec, that means a short walk to fetch his ‘squad.



(Boy) So, we’re getting Fizzers?



(Alec) We’re getting Fizzers. You always want Fizzers!



(Alec) So, I escort them, I walk with them to the court. I go to meet them at the schools and then walk them across from their schools down to the tennis courts. So, you also get to know them as you’re walking, making them feel comfortable trying to understand a little bit more about their life.



(Alec) Did you bring everything again? Is that your homework?



(Claire) Part coach, part chaperone… But it’s all in a day’s work for Alec.



(Claire) With every child who steps onto her courts, Ellis Park stirs back to life, and Alec’s dream of saving her feels closer than ever.



(Claire) What's the future for the Old Lady of Tennis?



(Alec) Liposuction. But yes… A facelift? We've made great progress with the application. The Heritage Foundation has accepted it with a proposal, and the City has accepted it. If anything, I'd love to see it to be as a museum – a museum of tennis in South Africa. The accolades, the brilliant players that we've had in memory, in honour of them. That is what I want.
